title: Week 14 · Lesson 38: Respiratory Pharmacology — Asthma, COPD & Inhaler Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 14 — Lesson 38: Respiratory Pharmacology — Asthma, COPD & Inhaler Safety

FNP-level goal: Use airway pathophysiology, phenotype, symptom pattern, inhaler technique, and illness severity to choose safer pharmacologic strategies for asthma and COPD—and recognize when outpatient care is unsafe.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish reliever, controller, and maintenance bronchodilator roles in asthma and COPD.
  • Explain why asthma therapy must address airway inflammation as well as bronchoconstriction.
  • Apply an inhaler-device and adherence assessment before escalating medication.
  • Compare LABA, LAMA, inhaled corticosteroid, and systemic corticosteroid roles and risks.
  • Recognize asthma and COPD exacerbation red flags requiring urgent or emergency evaluation.
  • Use smoking cessation, vaccination, action plans, and follow-up as medication-safety interventions.

Part 1 — Begin With the Syndrome, Not the Inhaler Name

Dyspnea, cough, wheeze, chest tightness, and reduced exercise tolerance are not diagnoses. Asthma, COPD, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, anemia, anxiety, upper-airway disease, medication adverse effects, and ischemia can overlap clinically.

Before adding an inhaler, ask: Is this asthma, COPD, an exacerbation, an alternative diagnosis, or more than one condition? Is the patient hypoxemic, fatigued, unable to speak comfortably, confused, cyanotic, hypotensive, or using accessory muscles? Stability comes before routine outpatient prescribing.

Part 2 — The Core Pharmacology of Airway Disease

Airway medications target different mechanisms:

  • Beta-2 agonists relax airway smooth muscle and improve bronchoconstriction.
  • Antimuscarinics reduce cholinergic bronchoconstriction and can support bronchodilation.
  • Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) reduce airway inflammation and exacerbation risk in appropriate asthma treatment.
  • Systemic corticosteroids may be used for selected acute exacerbations but have broad adverse effects.
  • Biologics and other add-on therapies are phenotype- and severity-specific and usually need specialist-directed assessment.

The same symptom—wheeze—does not prove that each medication class is appropriate.

Part 3 — Asthma: Inflammation and Variable Airflow Limitation

Asthma is characterized by variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation, with airway inflammation playing a central role for many patients. A bronchodilator can rapidly relieve constriction, but bronchodilation alone does not address the inflammatory risk that contributes to future severe exacerbations.

For this reason, current asthma strategies emphasize ICS-containing treatment rather than treating asthma as a SABA-only disease. The specific regimen depends on age, diagnosis certainty, symptom control, prior exacerbations, access, local formulary, device ability, comorbidities, and current guideline recommendations.

Part 4 — Reliever Versus Controller Thinking

A reliever is used for symptom relief. A controller is intended to reduce inflammation, future risk, and/or recurrent symptoms when used as prescribed. Some ICS-formoterol regimens can serve as an anti-inflammatory reliever, and in selected maintenance-and-reliever regimens the same inhaler is used for both scheduled maintenance and symptom relief.

Never assume that every ICS/LABA product can be used in every reliever strategy. Formulation, approved labeling, patient age, prescribed plan, and local guidance matter. Teach the exact inhaler name, purpose, frequency, and maximum-use instructions for that patient’s plan.

Part 5 — Excess Reliever Use Is Clinical Data

Frequent reliever use can signal poor control, incorrect technique, nonadherence to anti-inflammatory therapy, ongoing exposure, infection, an alternative diagnosis, or a developing exacerbation. It should prompt assessment—not automatic repeated refills.

Ask the patient to quantify use: “How many puffs, on how many days, and what was happening when you needed them?” Also ask about nocturnal symptoms, activity limitation, oral steroid bursts, urgent-care visits, ED visits, and hospitalizations.

Part 6 — Inhaler Technique Is Part of the Prescription

Medication cannot work if it does not reach the lungs. Metered-dose inhalers, dry-powder inhalers, soft-mist devices, spacers, and nebulized therapies require different techniques. Common failures include no exhalation before inhalation, incorrect inspiratory flow, poor timing with actuation, failure to hold the breath, and using an empty device.

At every new prescription and at follow-up, use teach-back: ask the patient to demonstrate the exact device. Do not merely ask, “Do you know how to use it?” A spacer may help selected patients using a metered-dose inhaler, but device choice must fit the patient’s dexterity, cognition, inspiratory capacity, affordability, and preference.

Part 7 — ICS Safety and Oral Care

ICS reduces exacerbation risk in appropriate asthma care, but it is not risk-free. Local adverse effects can include dysphonia and oral candidiasis. Patient education may include device-specific technique and rinsing/spitting after an ICS-containing inhaler when appropriate.

Persistent hoarseness, oral pain, white plaques, or poor response should trigger examination, technique review, adherence assessment, and consideration of other diagnoses—not unstructured dose escalation.

Part 8 — Acute Asthma: Assess Severity Before Adjusting a Home Plan

Worsening symptoms, low peak flow when used in an established plan, increasing reliever need, or reduced response to reliever medication may represent an exacerbation. Severe breathlessness at rest, inability to speak in full sentences, drowsiness, agitation, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, hypoxemia, or poor response to initial rescue therapy are emergency warning signs.

Do not ask an unstable patient to troubleshoot inhaler technique through a portal message. Arrange emergency evaluation according to severity and local protocols.

Part 9 — Systemic Corticosteroids: Useful, Not Casual

A short systemic corticosteroid course can be clinically appropriate for selected asthma or COPD exacerbations, but it has predictable risks: hyperglycemia, mood and sleep effects, blood-pressure and fluid effects, infection risk, dyspepsia, and cumulative HPA-axis exposure with repeated use.

Each burst is also a quality signal. Repeated systemic steroid exposure should prompt a review of diagnosis, trigger control, inhaler technique, adherence, maintenance treatment, access barriers, and need for pulmonary/allergy referral.

Part 10 — COPD: Persistent Airflow Limitation and Symptom Burden

COPD management differs from asthma management. In COPD, long-acting bronchodilation is often central to symptom relief and exacerbation prevention. Smoking exposure, occupational exposures, spirometric confirmation, symptom burden, prior exacerbations, eosinophil context, comorbidities, and inhaler technique all influence treatment decisions.

Do not label a patient with COPD solely because they smoke and wheeze. Diagnostic confirmation and a careful differential matter, especially when asthma features, heart failure, bronchiectasis, or recurrent infection are possible.

Part 11 — LABA and LAMA in COPD

Long-acting beta-2 agonists (LABA) and long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMA) provide sustained bronchodilation. In appropriate COPD patients, treatment may use one class or dual bronchodilation depending on symptoms, exacerbations, prior response, adverse effects, device feasibility, and current strategy recommendations.

Antimuscarinic adverse effects can include dry mouth and urinary symptoms. Beta-agonists can cause tremor or palpitations. New symptoms may reflect medication effects, but do not assume palpitations are benign in a patient with arrhythmia risk.

Part 12 — ICS in COPD Requires a Different Question

ICS may benefit selected COPD patients, particularly in certain exacerbation-risk and inflammatory contexts, but it is not automatically the first medication for every patient with COPD. ICS exposure can carry harms, including pneumonia risk in susceptible patients. The FNP should reassess the indication, prior exacerbations, asthma overlap, infection history, and current guidance rather than continuing an inhaler indefinitely by inertia.

Asthma and COPD have overlapping symptoms but are not pharmacologically interchangeable. Never transfer an asthma plan to COPD—or a COPD plan to asthma—without reassessing the diagnosis and risk.

Part 13 — COPD Exacerbation: Is It Airway Disease, Infection, or Another Emergency?

A COPD exacerbation is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms requiring additional therapy. It may be triggered by infection, pollution, nonadherence, or other factors. However, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, heart failure, pneumothorax, acute coronary syndrome, and arrhythmia can mimic or complicate it.

Assess change from baseline, respiratory rate and work of breathing, oxygenation, mental status, fever, sputum change, chest pain, edema, medication use, and access to home support. Antibiotics are not an automatic response to every cough; use current COPD guidance, clinical presentation, and evaluation for bacterial features or alternate diagnoses.

Part 14 — Oxygen Is a Treatment, Not a Reassurance Signal

Oxygen needs, target saturation, and escalation depend on the clinical setting, baseline disease, risk of hypercapnia, and local protocols. Low oxygen saturation, new confusion, severe work of breathing, or deterioration despite prescribed rescue therapy requires urgent assessment. Do not use a home pulse oximeter number in isolation to dismiss a visibly ill patient—or to manage a critical patient only by phone.

Part 15 — Smoking Cessation Is Respiratory Pharmacology

Tobacco cessation is one of the most effective disease-modifying interventions in COPD and improves overall cardiopulmonary risk. Treatment can include behavioral support and medication options chosen after reviewing tobacco use pattern, prior quit attempts, psychiatric history, seizure risk, pregnancy potential, drug interactions, contraindications, and patient preference.

A brief, specific plan is stronger than generic advice: identify a quit date, triggers, support person, medication plan when appropriate, and follow-up date. Relapse is common and should lead to re-engagement, not judgment.

Part 16 — Vaccination, Prevention, and Action Plans

Medication safety includes prevention. Review recommended respiratory vaccinations using current age-, condition-, and local guidance. For asthma, provide a written, individualized action plan when appropriate. For COPD, ensure the patient knows the baseline regimen, rescue plan, exacerbation warning signs, when to call, and when to seek emergency help.

Action plans must use the patient’s actual prescribed inhalers—not generic color zones copied from another patient.

Part 17 — Clinical Case: “My Rescue Inhaler Is Not Working”

A 29-year-old with asthma reports waking at night twice this week and using a rescue inhaler several times each day. They have not used their prescribed ICS-containing inhaler because it is “only for bad days.”

Build the mechanism: inadequate anti-inflammatory treatment + frequent symptoms → uncontrolled asthma and increased exacerbation risk. Confirm severity and stability, observe technique, clarify access and beliefs, review triggers and comorbidities, and create an individualized ICS-containing plan consistent with current guidance. If severe symptoms or emergency red flags are present, escalate immediately.

Part 18 — Clinical Case: COPD, Edema, and Breathlessness

A 71-year-old with COPD has increasing dyspnea, ankle edema, orthopnea, and a 6-pound weight gain. They request “a stronger inhaler.”

Do not anchor on COPD. Edema + orthopnea + rapid weight gain raise concern for heart failure and volume overload. The next step is a focused stability assessment and differential, not automatic bronchodilator escalation.

Part 19 — Clinical Case: Repeated Steroid Bursts

A patient has received four systemic steroid bursts for “bronchitis” in the past year. They have diabetes, insomnia, and osteoporosis risk.

FNP-level reasoning: repeated steroid exposure may reflect uncontrolled asthma/COPD, a missed alternative diagnosis, poor technique, poor access, or inadequate maintenance care. Review the cumulative harm, diagnosis, objective testing, inhaler use, triggers, and need for specialty support rather than repeating the same short-term rescue cycle.

FNP Respiratory Medication Framework

  1. Assess severity and emergency red flags before changing outpatient therapy.
  2. Confirm the working diagnosis and consider alternative causes of dyspnea or wheeze.
  3. Identify whether the medication goal is bronchodilation, inflammation control, exacerbation prevention, or smoking cessation.
  4. Review the exact device, technique, adherence, refill history, cost, and access barriers.
  5. Check adverse effects, comorbid cardiac disease, diabetes, infection risk, and medication interactions.
  6. Provide a written individualized action plan and explicit follow-up or escalation instructions.

High-Yield Summary

Asthma: airway inflammation matters; current strategies emphasize ICS-containing therapy rather than SABA-only treatment.
Inhaler technique: must be directly observed with teach-back.
Frequent reliever use: is a warning signal, not simply a refill request.
Systemic steroids: can be appropriate for selected exacerbations but repeated bursts create meaningful cumulative harm.
COPD: long-acting bronchodilation is central; ICS is individualized, not automatic.
Dyspnea: consider heart failure, PE, pneumonia, ischemia, and other dangerous alternatives.
Unstable respiratory symptoms: require urgent or emergency evaluation, not remote routine escalation.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Respiratory diagnosis, inhaler selection, dosing, acute-exacerbation management, oxygen use, antibiotics, systemic corticosteroids, and referral must follow current guidelines, prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
